title: Describing Words
subtitle: The Painter's Garden
intro: In the Painter's Garden, adjectives and adverbs mix their colors. Learn the secret order of adjectives, how to compare things, and when to say good or well.

rules.title: Order of Adjectives
rules.tagline: Opinion, size, age, shape, color, origin, material, purpose

story.line: Behold my wooden old big beautiful sword!
Pfft, that sounds broken. Like a robot sneezing.
Native speakers feel a secret order, even if they can't explain it. Opinion, size, age, shape, color, origin, material, purpose.
So: my beautiful big old wooden sword!
...That does sound way cooler.
Most sentences use only two or three adjectives, but the order still applies.

parts.name: 5. Color
parts.example: a lovely little old round red ...

parts.name: 6–8. Origin, material, purpose
parts.example: a lovely little old round red Japanese lacquer tea box

rules.history:
Nobody officially invented this order. It grew naturally, and native speakers follow it without being taught. Linguists think it reflects how 'built-in' a quality is: opinions change easily, so they go far from the noun; materials and purposes are almost part of the thing, so they sit right next to it.

In 2016, a passage from Mark Forsyth's book 'The Elements of Eloquence' (2013) went viral online, and suddenly millions of native speakers learned they had been following this rule all their lives.
rules.trick: OSASCOMP: Opinion, Size, Age, Shape, Color, Origin, Material, Purpose. Say it like a ninja spell: 'O-SAS-COMP!'

rules.title: Comparatives & Superlatives
rules.tagline: fast, faster, fastest / good, better, best

story.line: A race begins: Hana, Kaito and Yumi.
I'm fast! I'm more fast than Hana!
Faster, Kaito. Short words add -er.
And I'm the fastest of all! Hehe. Also the most intelligent.
Yumi knows: long words use more and most. Intelligent → more intelligent → the most intelligent.
Fine. But I'm the most best!
Never double up. Best is already the top.

parts.name: One syllable: -er / -est
parts.detail: Compare two with -er + than; the top of a group with the -est.

parts.name: Long words: more / most
parts.example: beautiful, more beautiful, the most beautiful

rules.history:
The -er and -est endings come straight from Old English (-ra and -ost). For a long time English used them on long words too, so writers wrote 'beautifullest.'

Under the influence of French and Latin, which compare with words like 'plus,' English began using more and most. By the 1700s, grammarians had settled on the modern split: short words take endings, long ones take more and most. Shakespeare could still write 'the most unkindest cut of all' for dramatic effect!

examples.good: This test is easier than the last one.
examples.bad: This test is more easy than the last one.

examples.good: She is the most talented singer here.
examples.bad: She is the talentedest singer here.

examples.good: My cooking is worse than yours.
examples.bad: My cooking is badder than yours.

rules.trick: Short word? Stick on a tail (-er, -est). Long word? Give it a hat (more, most). Never both.

quiz.q: 'That was the ___ day of my life!'

rules.title: Good vs. Well
rules.tagline: Good describes nouns; well describes actions

story.line: Sensei! Did I fight good today?
You fought well. Fight is a verb, so it needs the adverb well.
So I'm not a good fighter?
You are a good fighter. Fighter is a noun, so the adjective good is correct.
What about 'I feel good'?
Feel is a linking verb, so 'I feel good' (happy) is right. 'I feel well' usually means 'I'm not sick.' Both work, with different meanings.

parts.name: Good = adjective
parts.detail: Describes a noun or follows a linking verb.
parts.example: a good book; The food smells good.

parts.name: Well = adverb
parts.detail: Describes how an action is done.

parts.name: Well = healthy
parts.detail: Well can also be an adjective meaning healthy.

parts.name: Same pattern
parts.detail: Other adjective/adverb pairs work the same way.

rules.history:
Good and well have been separate words since Old English (gōd and wel). Well was always an adverb, just as it is today.

In casual American speech, 'You did good' became common in the 1900s, especially in sports. It's widely heard but still considered informal; in writing, 'You did well' is the safe choice.

examples.good: You did well on the test.
examples.bad: You did good on the test.
examples.note: Did is an action verb → well (formal writing).
Tastes is a linking verb → good.

rules.trick: Superman does good; you do well. Actions get well, things are good.

rules.title: Where Adverbs Go
rules.tagline: Frequency adverbs before the main verb, after be

story.line: I tell always the truth!
Hmm, both the grammar and the statement are suspicious.
Frequency adverbs like always, often, never usually sit right before the main verb: I always tell the truth.
But 'I am always hungry' has always after am!
Correct! With the verb be, the adverb comes after it. And with helpers: I have never seen a dragon.

parts.name: Before the main verb
parts.detail: always, usually, often, sometimes, rarely, never.

parts.name: After the first helper
parts.example: I have always wanted a cat.

parts.name: Manner at the end
parts.detail: How adverbs usually go after the verb and object.

parts.name: Not between verb and object
parts.detail: Don't split a verb from its object.
parts.example: He speaks English fluently. (not speaks fluently English)

rules.history:
English adverbs are some of the most mobile words in the language. Old English placed them quite freely.

As word order became fixed (subject-verb-object), adverbs got squeezed into certain slots so they wouldn't break the S-V-O chain. That's why 'I like very much sushi' sounds wrong: it splits the verb from its object.

examples.good: I usually wake up at seven.
examples.bad: I wake up usually at seven.

rules.trick: Adverb of frequency = a little bodyguard. It stands in front of action verbs, but behind the king verb 'be.'
